records.our_prose: Cane management is the heart of growing blackberries, because the crown and roots are perennial but each cane is biennial: it grows one year as a primocane, fruits the next as a floricane, then dies. How you prune depends on both habit and cane type. On ERECT SUMMER-BEARING types, tip the primocanes at 3 to 4 feet in summer to force fruiting laterals; the next year those canes fruit as floricanes and then die, so cut spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest, and in late winter shorten the laterals to 12 to 18 inches and thin to 4 to 6 sturdy canes per foot of row. Erect types also sucker from the roots and need their spread contained to the row. On SEMI-ERECT and TRAILING types, which form a crown and do not sucker, train the long primocanes onto a trellis through the season, remove spent floricanes after harvest, and in late winter shorten laterals (about 10 to 12 inches on semi-erect) and keep 6 to 8 strong canes per crown. On PRIMOCANE-FRUITING (everbearing) types, the first-year canes fruit on their tips in late summer and fall; the simplest management is to mow every cane to the ground in late winter for one clean, heavy fall crop with the easiest pruning and reduced disease and borer pressure. The same planting can instead be double-cropped, leaving the lower canes to fruit again as floricanes the next summer, but the single-crop mow is the usual home choice.

records.our_prose: Feed blackberries in early spring when growth starts, using a balanced fertilizer or some composted manure spread along the row, and again lightly right after you finish picking. That feeding fuels the new canes for next year. Go easy late in the season, since too much makes weak, floppy canes.

records.our_prose: Blackberries are hardy in roughly zones 5 to 9, less cold-tolerant than raspberries but far more heat-tolerant, which is why they are the caneberry of the South. Cold hardiness follows habit: erect and semi-erect types are the toughest (Illini Hardy, Apache, and Chester are the standouts, reliable to about zone 5 and the edge of zone 4), while trailing types (marionberry, boysenberry) are the most tender and can be injured below about 13 °F, suiting them to mild coastal regions. In the far North (zones 3 to 4) blackberries are marginal and need winter protection; at the warm end, low-chill types thrive through the Deep South, and only the frost-free tropics push past their need for winter chill.

records.source_context: Blackberries often suffer from some cold injury in northern Utah, which typically results in loss of floricane buds, or dieback of the entire cane (Figure 1). As a general rule, trailing types of blackberries are the most cold sensitive, and semi-erect types are the most cold hardy. Although Utah winter conditions rarely cause permanent damage to the plant, floricane damage reduces or eliminates potential yields.

records.our_prose: Blackberries prefer a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerate about 5.5 to 7.0. This is close to what most vegetable gardens already carry, so no special acidification is needed, unlike a blueberry. In strongly alkaline soils above about 7.5 the plants can develop iron chlorosis (yellowing between the veins), best corrected with added organic matter and a chelated-iron product rather than a drastic pH change.
records.source_context: Establishing the Planting Soils Caneberries grow best in deep, sandy loam soils rich in organic matter. Ideal soil should have a pH of 6.0 to 6.5 and be well-drained to a depth of at least 3 feet. Caneberries are sensitive to excess waterlogging, and even temporary water accumulation can weaken canes, hinder plant growth, and increase incidences of diseases — particularly root rots.

records.our_prose: Plant dormant bare-root canes so the roots are an inch or two deep, then cut the old cane back to a few inches. Plant in late winter or early spring in cold areas, or over winter where winters are mild. Space upright types about 2 to 4 feet apart, and the big arching or trailing types about 6 to 8 feet apart, in rows 8 to 10 feet apart. Use a slightly raised, well-drained row in full sun, and put up the trellis before the canes grow.
source_names: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
records.source_context: If possible, rows should be oriented north to south so that both sides of the blackberry plant will receive even sunlight, ensuring maximum production and ripening of the fruit. Semi-trailing varieties should be planted 6 to 8 feet apart in the row, with rows 10 feet apart. Erect varieties should be planted 2 to 4 feet apart in the row and 10 feet between rows.

records.our_prose: Plant dormant bare-root canes, setting the crown so the roots sit 1 to 2 inches below the surface, then cut the old handle cane back to a few inches. Plant in late winter or early spring in the North, or from late fall through winter in mild regions. Space erect types about 2 to 4 feet apart, and the vigorous semi-erect and trailing types about 6 to 8 feet apart, in rows 8 to 10 feet apart. Plant on a slightly raised, well-drained row in full sun and install the trellis before growth begins; only compact erect types can be grown without support.

records.our_prose: The Mid-South is prime blackberry country, and Arkansas is its home turf. The University of Arkansas fruit breeding program developed most of the thornless upright cultivars grown across the state, and blackberries thrive in both the Ozark uplands and the lowland South, fruiting heavily from late spring into summer. Plant dormant canes over winter into early spring, give them a simple trellis, watch for rosette disease, and cut out the old fruited canes each year. Winters here are far more than cold enough, so chill is never something to worry about.

records.our_prose: Summer-bearing (floricane-fruiting) blackberry is the type to grow across the Ozark uplands, and it is squarely at home here: the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program developed most of the state's standard cultivars. Thornless erect and semi-erect types (Ouachita, Navaho, Apache) are the easiest to pick and manage, and chill is never a limiter, since even the highest-chill University of Arkansas releases (about 800 to 900 hours) are cleared many times over by the uplands' winter.

records.our_prose: Get the row ready before you plant, in a full-sun spot. Most garden soil is fine; aim for a pH around 6.0 to 6.5 and only adjust if it is far off. Mix in plenty of compost or aged manure, and on heavy or wet soil, plant on a raised mound so the roots stay dry. Pull out weeds and any wild brambles nearby, and avoid spots that recently grew tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries.

records.our_prose: Keep the soil consistently moist, about 1 to 2 inches of water per week, more in heat. The most water-sensitive window runs from bloom through harvest, when the developing berries need steady moisture to size and stay plump.
records.source_context: Water and Fertilizer Blackberries require frequent irrigation during the growing season, ensuring they are always moist but not saturated. Provide 1-2 inches of water per week from mid-May through October, irrigating two times per week. Overhead irrigation is not recommended as it promotes fruit rot and other diseases Fertilize with annual application of nitrogen fertilizer prior to growing season in January.
